rationale: A wins because it is tougher on its own material: "A profitable public company is giving away chess and charging for the AI" gives a real market protagonist, a business-model tension, and the proof a reporter would demand. B has usable bones, but lines like "the 'what gets gated' question showing up across consumer subscription products" borrow a trend it has not earned, and "Behind Duolingo's record user growth: two new bets and a profitable balance sheet" starts smelling like padded stock-story garnish. A still needs a fact scrub, but it has sharper editorial judgment.
gaps_in_A: "cartoon owl" is the wrong protagonist for the supplied facts; the update says users talk with Lily, not the owl.
"most-criticized design" inflates "some educators have publicly criticized gamification" into an unsupported superlative.
"the beta number is being published for the first time" is invented; the update says there was a beta and gives the metric, not first publication status.
"The language app that decided it isn't a language app" overstates the category break; one chess course does not prove Duolingo has redefined itself.
gaps_in_B: "engagement is at an all-time high" conflates record DAU with engagement; the update only says DAU hit a new high and beta video sessions averaged 9 minutes.
"a live public educator critique" makes a standing criticism sound current; no dated educator event is supplied.
"the 'what gets gated' question showing up across consumer subscription products" creates an industry-trend peg without evidence in the update.
"same quarter" and "ahead of earnings" are invented market timing; the update gives a current launch, profitability, and DAU growth, not an earnings setup.
